Revised 2026-10-23 after persona review: m7 reframed to IM's answer to question 4 (Kiran is right about the meeting time, but the meeting place would move to Clare's house), so “he's not correct” is treated as possibly part right; Premo's example numbers (21, 21–18–15, 11:75, the m9 displays) now say in `means` or `why` that they are examples, not IM's; the language moment and cruxLanguage now ask every level the same question (what can be counted or measured) and the same reasoning (how the distance apart changes each hour, and why), with home language offered at every level; jargon replaced with plain words in teacher-facing text (readiness check, MLR1, Three Reads, presentations, extension, Notice and Wonder, combined speed); moments that point at a question now say what it asks; beforeClass trimmed to short tasks, the in-class pick of student work dropped, a four-column table added for m5.

Crux is 8.2, the lesson's only full activity (30 minutes). Both of IM's goals land there: using speed to find unknown distances and times, and interpreting a story about two objects moving at constant speeds and making a diagram or table for it. 8.1 is the warm-up and 8.3 is optional practice (IM: “more opportunity to practice”).

Testable object: the distance-apart table (question 2 of 8.2: how far apart after 0, 1, 2 and 3 hours). The meeting time, Kiran's 6.4 miles per hour claim and the jogging question all rest on seeing that the gap shrinks by 6.4 miles each hour. IM's launch protects it too: display a solution to the first two problems before groups move on.

IM's own moments used: the distance-apart misconception (IM's four-column table), the time-reading misconception, the Three Reads support at the 8.2 launch, the Group Presentations restate line from IM's routine definition, MLR1's press-for-details, the Three Reads breakdown from the routine catalog, the share order in 8.2's synthesis, and the speed/pace mix-up in 8.3. The 12 ÷ 75 moment in 8.1 rests on the unit readiness check, item 6, whose move points at “Lesson 8 Activity 1”; I read that as the warm-up 8.1, where 12/75 = 0.16 is needed.

Premo's moments: the reading of Kiran's claim as his real speed, and the 9.6 miles per hour answer to the jogging question. The by-level moves in the language moment and in cruxLanguage are all Premo's; IM gives one support for everyone.

Example values that are mine, not IM's: “21” in the 1-hour row (24 − 3, one walker only) illustrates IM's distance-apart misconception; “11:75, so 12:15” applies IM's time misconception (its example is 2.5 hours after 8 a.m. is 10:30, not 10:50) to question 3, because in question 5 the clock time is given and the hours are what students work out.

IM's synthesis says to start “from the most common strategies” and move to the least common, but each group presents a different assigned problem. It is not clear whether the order is by problem or by strategy within a problem. The sequence in inClass is written as an order to apply to what the teacher sees, not a claim about which way is most common.

IM's English-learner support says to “reveal the first three questions” on the third read; the launch says quiet think time on “the first two questions” and then a display of solutions to those two. I followed the launch.

Example values that are mine, not IM's: “21” in the 1-hour row and “21, 18, 15” in the patterns (24 − 3 each hour, one walker only) illustrate IM's distance-apart misconception; “11:75, so 12:15” applies IM's time misconception (its example is 2.5 hours after 8 a.m. is 10:30, not 10:50) to question 3, because in question 5 the clock time is given and the hours are what students work out; the displays in m9 and “24 ÷ 3” in m3 are examples too. Each says so in its `means` or `why`.

8.2's purpose is recorded in the IM layer as application, read from the optional modeling sentence (MP4). Its first sentence (“answer questions in the context of constant speed”) could also read as practice. That does not change the crux, since 8.3 is the optional one.
Student responses and the cool-down were transcribed from the Teacher Guide page images by a model, not checked by a person.

Revised 2026-10-24: routine centred; copy edit. Added m12, a rehearsed run-routine moment for Three Reads (MLR 6) at the 8.2 launch (say line, a three-step run sheet, one step per read; IM gives no minutes for the reads, so none are listed; evidence is IM’s “without solving it for students” sentence). The third step follows the launch (first two questions), as noted above. m3, the Three Reads breakdown (“Students start calculating on the first read.”), is now rehearsed. Un-rehearsed m10 (Group Presentations) and m6 (time reading), criteria dropped, to keep six rehearsed: m1 and m2 upstream, m12, m3, m4 and m5 at the crux. m4 stays as the level-specific support during the second read; m12 is the teacher running all three. predict.tell now says the sixth moment (m5). inClass.momentIds now m12, m4, m5. cruxLanguage.byBand: added does and reaching; entries rewritten as one short sentence per read. Routines named with MLR numbers on first mention (cruxWhy, m2, m3, m4, m10, m12, cuts); beforeClass items labelled with the routine they serve. Copy edits: “30-minute question”; cruxWhy parallel fixed; rates as “per” (miles per minute, minutes per mile, miles per hour); times as “8 a.m.”, “10:30 a.m.”, “11:45 a.m.”; “0.75 hours” throughout m6; 12/75 written as \(\frac{12}{75}\) in m1; “mathematics” → “math”; one home-language sentence in m4 and cruxLanguage; “English learners” → “multilingual learners” in cruxWhy. Numbers rechecked: 12/75 = 0.16; 24 − 3 − 3.4 = 17.6; 24 ÷ 6.4 = 3.75 hours = 3 hours 45 minutes, so 11:45 a.m.; 24 ÷ 2.5 = 9.6, 9.6 − 3.4 = 6.2.

cruxWhy: 8.2 is where both of IM’s goals are met: students use speeds to find unknown distances and times, and interpret a written story of two friends moving at constant speeds by making a table. IM gives it 30 minutes, supports multilingual learners with Three Reads (MLR 6), in which the class reads the story three times, and has each group explain a problem to the class. 8.1 warms up the speed and pace ideas; 8.3 is optional practice.

object.name: the distance-apart table
object.what: The table each student makes of how far apart Kiran and Clare are after 0, 1, 2 and 3 hours. The next questions test it: when do they meet, and what does Kiran mean by 6.4 miles per hour?

goal: Students use speed to find unknown distances and times, explain how, and turn a story about two friends walking toward each other into a table they can reason from.
rigorCheck: Does every student still make the distance-apart table, use it to find when the friends meet, and decide whether Kiran’s 6.4 miles per hour idea holds?

watchFor.8.1: A student writes “12 ÷ 75” and stops there.
watchFor.8.2: The 1-hour row of the distance-apart table takes off only Kiran’s 3 miles, giving 21, for example.
watchFor.8.3: “The cousin is faster, 24 is more than 6.”

moments.see: For the 30-minute question, a student writes “12 ÷ 75” and stops: “That doesn’t come out even.”
moments.means: \(\frac{12}{75}\) is 0.16 miles per minute, but only once they see it as hundredths. IM’s check at the start of the unit flags this fraction-to-decimal step for today’s warm-up.
moments.say: Twelve out of 75. What would that be out of 100?
moments.dont: Do the division on the board for them.
moments.evidence: plan to attend to the relationship between fractions and decimals in Lesson 8 Activity 1
criteria: Kept the decimal step with the student
Linked \(\frac{12}{75}\) to a fraction they can already write as a decimal
Didn’t do the division for them

moments.routine: MLR1: Stronger and Clearer Each Time
moments.see: New partners compare: “4.8.” “Same.” “Cool.” They turn around.
moments.means: In Stronger and Clearer Each Time (MLR 1), students explain to a new partner each time, and matching answers end the talk. The partner swap is for pressing each other on how, so the explanation gets clearer before the class discussion.
moments.say: Same answer. Now ask how they got it.
moments.dont: Move on because the answers match.
moments.evidence: students should be pressed for details, and encouraged to press each other for details.
criteria: Sent partners to each other’s reasoning, not the answer
Asked for a detail: a step, a unit or a rate
Didn’t move on because the answers matched

moments.see: The Kiran and Clare story is up with its questions covered. Groups are seated, books closed, waiting for you to start.
moments.means: Three Reads (MLR 6) means reading the same story three times, each time for one thing, so students understand it before they solve. IM uses it here to support reading the word problem without solving it for students. On the first read, listen for the situation in words: two friends walking toward each other for a picnic. On the second, listen for the quantities and rates: 24 miles apart, 3 miles per hour, 3.4 miles per hour. Amplify that language of quantities and rates; IM says it connects the story’s words with the reasoning students need for the table.
moments.say: We’ll read this story three times, each time for something different.

runSheet.step: First read: students say what is happening, with no numbers.
Second read: students name what can be counted or measured, with units.
Third read: show the first two questions, then give quiet think time.

moments.dont: Solve any part of the problem during the reads.
moments.evidence: Use this routine to support reading comprehension of this word problem, without solving it for students.
criteria: Gave each read its own job, in order
Kept numbers out of the first read
Didn’t solve any part of the problem during the reads

moments.see: On the first read of the story, students start calculating: pencils are already working 24 ÷ 3.
moments.means: In Three Reads (MLR 6), the first read is for the story only. Calculating now skips knowing what is going on and what is asked. (24 ÷ 3 is an example.)
moments.say: No numbers yet. What is happening in this story?
moments.dont: Let the fastest calculators set the pace.
moments.evidence: To ensure that students know what they are being asked to do
criteria: Sent the class back to the story, not the numbers
Asked what is happening, in words
Didn’t let the fastest calculators set the pace

moments.see: On the second read, a student points at “3.4” and says nothing.
moments.means: This is the second read of Three Reads (MLR 6). They have found a quantity. Saying what it measures, and whose it is, is the reading work this read asks for.

emerging.say: What can be counted or measured here? Point and show me.
emerging.move: They point to each number in the story and show what it measures and whose it is, with a word, a gesture or a sketch. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.
emerging.nonverbal: Point to the number, then to Kiran or Clare in the story, then to the photo of the trail.

developing.say: What can be counted or measured here? Tell your partner.
developing.move: They tell a partner what each number measures and whose it is, with its unit, using “___ is ___ miles per hour.” They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.

expanding.say: What can be counted or measured here? Tell your partner each one.
expanding.move: They tell a partner, in their own sentences, what each number measures and whose it is, with its unit. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.

moments.dont: Tell them what the number means.
moments.evidence: Use the second read to identify the important quantities by asking students what can be counted or measured
criteria: Kept the same question at every level: what can be counted or measured
Matched the way in to the student’s level
Didn’t tell them what the number means

moments.see: The 1-hour row of the distance-apart table says 21. “Kiran walked 3, so 24 take away 3.”
moments.means: They tracked one walker. Both friends close the gap each hour, so it shrinks by 3 and by 3.4. IM names this trouble with distance apart; the 21 is an example.
moments.say: Where is Clare after one hour? Show both of them.
moments.evidence: Students who are unsure about how to calculate distance apart in the table may benefit from creating a table with 4 columns: time in hours, how far Kiran has traveled, how far Clare has traveled, and the distance between them.
criteria: Asked about both friends, not just one
Offered a sketch of the trail or a column for each walker
Didn’t fix the 1-hour row for them

moments.see: “3.75 hours after 8 a.m. They meet at 11:75, so 12:15.”
moments.means: They read 3.75 hours as 3 hours 75 minutes. 0.75 hours is 45 minutes, so the picnic is at 11:45 a.m. IM’s example is 2.5 hours after 8 a.m. read as 10:50 a.m.; 11:75 is an example on the meeting-time question.
moments.say: 0.75 hours. How many minutes is that?
moments.evidence: Look for students misinterpreting expressions of time. For example, 2.5 hours after 8 a.m. is 10:30 a.m., not 10:50 a.m.

moments.see: On the question asking whether Kiran is right that walking toward each other is like Clare staying put while he jogs 6.4 miles per hour: “He’s not correct. He walks 3.”
moments.means: Maybe part right. Kiran doesn’t walk 6.4; he means the gap closes 6.4 miles each hour, so they meet at the same time. IM’s answer adds that the meeting place would change, to Clare’s house. Find out which part the student means.
moments.say: Same meeting time? Same meeting place? Which part is wrong?
moments.dont: Mark “not correct” wrong without asking why.

moments.see: On the question asking how fast Kiran jogged if they met at 10:30 a.m.: “24 ÷ 2.5 = 9.6. Kiran jogged 9.6 miles per hour.”
moments.means: 9.6 is how fast the gap closed, both friends together. Clare’s 3.4 is still inside it.
moments.say: Is 9.6 Kiran alone, or both of them?

moments.see: On the displays: a trail sketch with miles marked off, two-column tables, a four-column table, one “9.6 − 3.4.”
moments.means: IM starts the class discussion from the most common way and moves to the least common, pointing out unit rates, scaling and tables as they come. The displays above are an example of what you might see.
moments.say: Start us off. How did your group set up the table?
moments.evidence: If possible, start from the most common strategies and move to the least common.

moments.see: A group finishes explaining whether Kiran is right that it’s like him jogging 6.4 miles per hour. You ask, “Any questions?” Silence.
moments.means: In Group Presentations, “Any questions?” lets everyone off. Putting the group’s finding in their own words is how the rest of the class takes it in.
moments.say: Who can say what this group found, in your words?
moments.dont: Fill the silence by explaining it again yourself.
moments.evidence: instead of asking if anyone has any questions for the group, it is often more productive to ask a member of the class to restate their understanding of the group’s findings in their own words.

moments.see: “The cousin is faster. 24 is more than 6.”
moments.means: They compared paces as if they were speeds. More minutes for each mile is slower.
moments.say: Label the units. What does 24 minutes per mile mean?
moments.evidence: Some students may confuse the meaning of the speed and pace, thinking that 24 minutes per mile is faster than 6 minutes per mile.

patterns.why: The rate is right; writing 12/75 as a decimal is the step in the way.
patterns.shows: They know speed means miles for each minute.
patterns.evidence: For this task students will need to be fluent in their use of fractions and decimals to make sense of unit rates and scaling.

patterns.why: They scale down the time column and do the same to the miles.
patterns.shows: Equivalent ratios without a unit rate at all.

patterns.why: They used the pace, the other unit rate, to find a distance.
patterns.shows: Both unit rates, and that dividing by the pace works too.

patterns.says: 21, then 18, then 15 in the distance-apart table.
patterns.why: An example of IM’s distance-apart trouble: only Kiran’s 3 miles per hour is taken off.
patterns.shows: They can use a speed to step the table hour by hour.
patterns.evidence: Students who are unsure about how to calculate distance apart in the table

patterns.why: They see the same drop in each row of the distance-apart table.
patterns.shows: The idea behind the meeting time and the question about Kiran’s 6.4 miles per hour.
patterns.evidence: the distance between them is decreasing by 6.4 miles each hour

patterns.why: An example of IM’s time mix-up: the decimal part of an hour is read as minutes.
patterns.shows: They found 3.75 hours, which is right.
patterns.evidence: Look for students misinterpreting expressions of time.

patterns.why: They add the two speeds and use that directly.
patterns.shows: Kiran’s 6.4 miles per hour idea, used on the question of how fast he jogged.
patterns.evidence: then their combined speed is 9.6 miles per hour

patterns.shows: They see the gap closing, which is the idea of the table.

predict.context: Kiran and Clare live 24 miles apart on a rail trail and start walking toward each other at 8 a.m., Kiran at 3 miles per hour and Clare at 3.4. After quiet think time, students find how far apart they are after one hour, then make a table of how far apart they are after 0, 1, 2 and 3 hours.
predict.question: What will most students’ distance-apart tables look like?
predict.countQuestion: How many students will have 17.6 miles in the 1-hour row?
predict.countUnit: students will have 17.6 miles in the 1-hour row.
predict.tell: If few do, the distance-apart table is following one walker, and the meeting time and the question about Kiran’s 6.4 miles per hour have nothing to stand on. That is the sixth moment you’ll rehearse.

emerging.entry: First read: they tell the story with gestures or a sketch. Second read: they point to each number and show what it measures. Third read: on a trail sketch, they show how much closer the friends get each hour, and why. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.
emerging.frame: Kiran’s speed is ___. Clare’s speed is ___. Each hour they get ___ miles closer.
emerging.does: They can follow a story of two people moving and match each number to the right person.
emerging.reaching: Showing that both friends close the gap each hour, using the word speed.
emerging.stretch: They say each number with its unit: “3 miles per hour.”

developing.entry: First read: they tell a partner the story. Second read: they name each quantity with its unit. Third read: they say how the distance apart changes each hour, and why, using speed. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.
developing.frame: Each hour they get ___ miles closer, because Kiran’s speed is ___ and Clare’s speed is ___.
developing.does: They can name each friend’s speed with its unit, such as 3 miles per hour.
developing.reaching: Saying in a sentence why the distance apart shrinks by both speeds each hour.
developing.stretch: They join the two speeds in one sentence: together they close 6.4 miles each hour.

expanding.entry: First read: they retell the story. Second read: they name each quantity with its unit. Third read: they say how the distance apart changes each hour, and why, using speed. They can work it out first in any language they share with a partner.
expanding.frame: Each hour, the distance apart ___ because ___.
expanding.does: They can retell the story and name every quantity with its unit.
expanding.reaching: Explaining why the gap closes 6.4 miles each hour and using that to judge Kiran’s idea.
expanding.stretch: They predict when the friends meet from the gap and the combined speed, before calculating.

cuts.note: Optional, more practice with no new math. Cut it first.
Keep it short: two questions, one partner swap in Stronger and Clearer Each Time (MLR 1), then name speed and pace.

Skip the extra challenge problem and the optional Notice and Wonder opening, where students say what they notice and wonder. Keep Three Reads (MLR 6), the quiet think time, showing answers to the first two questions, and each group explaining its problem (Group Presentations).

neverCut: Quiet think time on the first two questions
Showing a distance-apart table before groups move on
The question on Kiran’s 6.4 miles per hour idea
Each group explaining its problem to the class

inClass.launch: “How far apart after one hour? Then make the distance-apart table.”
sequence: The way most groups used, as you saw it while walking around
Less common ways: a sketch of the trail with miles marked off, a four-column table
The least common: adding the two speeds (6.4, or 9.6 on the question of how fast Kiran jogged) and using that directly

beforeClass: For the launch: look up a rail trail near school to tell students about.
For Three Reads (MLR 6): set up the Kiran and Clare story to show with its questions covered.
For Group Presentations: poster paper and markers, one set per group of 3–4.
For Group Presentations: decide which group explains each of questions 3, 4 and 5.
For the distance-apart table: draw a blank four-column table (hours, Kiran, Clare, distance apart) for students who need it.
